title: A catalyst based on copper-cadmium bimetal for electrochemical reduction of CO2 to CO with high faradaic efficiency
abstract: Electrochemical reduction carbon dioxide (CO2) can produce value-added chemicals such as carbon monoxide and hydrocarbon. However, the sluggish kinetic process and complex reaction routes of CO2 electro-reduction reaction (CO2RR) largely limit the conversion efficiency and products selectivity. Herein, a Cu2Cd/Cd/Cu bimetallic catalyst by imbedding Cd bulks onto Cu substrate surface was designed and applied for the CO2RR. This catalyst presents good conductivity and selectivity toward the CO2RR. Particularly, the catalyst shows CO conversion faradaic efficiency of 84% with a current density of 8 mA cm at -1.0 V vs. RHE in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution. Detailed investigation has revealed that the electrocatalytic capability of this catalyst can be attributed to the boundaries between Cu and Cd that could provide sufficient active sites for the CO2RR and the formation of Cu2Cd alloy that could enhance the binding energy between the catalyst and the intermediate.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Converting CO2 into value-added chemicals and useful fuels could reduce the CO2 level in the atmosphere as well as to mitigate the environmental issues such as climate change and ocean acidification.[1,2] In recent years, the CO2 electro-reduction reaction (CO2RR) has attracted increasing research interests, owing to the moderate reaction condition and high energy density products, including carbon monoxide and hydrocarbon.[3,4] The aim of CO2RR is contingent on finding electrocatalysts with capability of efficiently converting CO2 into a single product with high faradaic efficiency. However, the selectivity of the CO2RR is low, which can be reflected by their products being generally a mixture of carbon compounds, including CO, HCOO-, CH4, C2H4, C2H5OH, and CH3OH. [5,6] Among them, CO is one of the desired products, because it could serve as an important raw material in chemical process industry to produce many kinds of chemicals and synthetic fuels.[7-9] Typically, the CO2RR process involves three major steps: i) chemical adsorption of CO2 on electrocatalysts; ii) electron transfer and/or proton migration to cleave C-O bonds and/or form C-H
bonds; and iii) configuration rearrangement of products to desorb them from the electrocatalyst surface and diffuse into the electrolyte.[10] Owing to the fact that the
CO2 molecule is fully oxide and extremely stable, a high overpotential is required to cleave C-O bonds. Meanwhile, the H2 evolution reaction suppress the CO2RR whenever the overpotential is too high or too low. There are various approaches in
configuration rearrangement of products at the moderate overpotential. Thus the
selectivity of the product for the CO2RR is not high. Researchers have thought about

replacing the electrolyte of aqueous solution with the ionic liquid to avoid the
evolution of H2 as well as increase the solubility of CO2 to enhance the selectivity of the product.[11] Besides, the catalyst providing more active sites for the CO2RR has high selectivity, so many researchers are devoted to synthesize catalysts owning high specific surface area.[12] In addition, the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER),
occurring at around 0 V (versus RHE) depending on electrolytes, usually competes
with the CO2RR in which CO forms at -0.1 V (versus RHE) in aqueous solution. Therefore, the catalysts with the property of suppressing HER are highly desirable for the CO2RR. [13, 14]
Highly conductive single metals, such Au, Ag, and Pd exhibit good performance for
the CO2RR in terms of high selectivity, but they usually suffer from large overpotential, poisoning, and high price.[15-19] Compared with single metal catalysts as
mentioned above, bimetallic compounds could modulate the chemical environment of
electrode surface, and thus reduce the energy difference between CO2 and intermediates, eventually offering low overpotential for corresponding reactions.[20] -
Meanwhile the synthesis of bimetallic compounds could become a good approach to
replace the edge atoms of single metal preferentially absorbing H2 with another metal atoms which absorb CO2, and thus suppress the competitive HER over the direct CO2RR. One can take advantage of electronic affinity brought by different metals for adsorption of oxygen atom and carbon atoms, which plays a crucial role in
determining the binding energy of the intermediate such as *COOH and *OCHO on
corresponding metals. These different intermediates determine different products such

as CO and formic acid.[21] Consequently, the selectivity of electrocatalysts can be
largely enhanced by tuning the binding energy of intermediates on catalysts through
bimetallic compounds compositions. For instance, Bao et al. reported
copper-palladium bimetallic electrocatalysts that could convert CO2 to CO with faradaic efficiency of 86%. The electrode achieved current density of 6.9 mA cm−2 and mass activity of 24.5 A g−1 at −0.89 V vs. RHE in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 solution.[22] Cu-Sn with core/shell structure has also shown striking CO2-to-CO activities, reaching 95% faradaic efficiency of CO2 converting to CO at -0.7 V (vs. RHE).[23] Takanabe et al., reported copper-indium bimetallic electrocatalysts that could convert CO2 to CO with a faradaic efficiency of 90% at -0.5 V vs. RHE. [24] In short, these Cu-based bimetallic catalysts display excellent performance towards the
CO2RR. However, the complex preparation process and the not good enough durability of only several hours are the main disadvantages for the above catalysts.
In addition, in view of mostly reported bimetallic catalysts for the CO2RR, the electrodes consist of late transition metals with filled d-orbital, such as Cu, Ag, Au,
and Zn, etc., and those composed of two different metals have exhibited good performance toward the CO2RR. [25-28] Among these metals, Cu is a non-precious and good conductive late transition metal. Initial oxidation pre-treatment of Cu electrode
could generate high surface area with grain boundaries, which is good for improving selectivity for CO conversion.[29] Furthermore, the bimetallic catalysts consisting of Cu and Zn or In have shown high selectivity of CO towards the CO2RR. [30, 31]
Herein, we report on Cd/Cu bimetallic material used as catalyst for CO2 reduction

2. Experimental section
2.1 Materials
Copper foil (100 µm in thickness, 99.99%, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as substrates
for catalysts. Cadmium chloride (CdCl2·2.5 H2O, 95%, Chem-Supply), citric acid monohydrate (C6H8O7·H2O, 99%, Chem-Supply) were used in the deposition of Cd
M AN
US CR
IP T

PT ED
on Cu foils. Potassium bicarbonate (KHCO3, 99.0%, Chem-Supply) was used for electrolyte.
2.2 Cu2Cd/Cd/Cu electrode fabrication
To fabricate thick films of the Cu-Cd bimetallic electrodes, Cu foils were cut to
the desired electrode size (1×2 cm2) and placed in a Teflon shelf to separate from each
other firstly. Thereafter, the foils were immersed into 3 M HCl for 2 hours to remove
the oxide layer of the Cu surface. Then the foils were sonicated in deionized water,
ethanol and acetone for each 15 min by turns, and dried under nitrogen gas. The
treated electrodes were placed vertically in a ceramic crucible and thermally oxidized at 773 K for 2 h at the heating rate of 2 ℃ min-1 under static air in a muffle furnace.
After calcination, the Cu foils were evenly covered with CuxO particles as shown in Fig. S1. Thereafter, the Cd/Cu electrode was prepared through the in situ
electrochemical reduction of the thermally oxidized Cu electrodes in 20 ml solution
containing 0.05 M CdCl2/0.4 M citric acid (sonicated 15 min before deposition, area immersed into the solution is 1×1 cm2) at a constant current of -10 mA for 1 h. Then
the fabricated electrode was cleaned with deionized water several times, and it was
treated electrochemically at the potential of -1.65 V (vs. SCE) in 0.1 M KHCO3 solution saturated with N2 for 45 min.
2.3 Structural characterization

process of deposition and electrochemical treatment were observed using a Sirion 200

2.4 Electrochemical measurements
All the electrochemical measurements were conducted in a typical three-electrode
setup with a potentiostat (CH Instrument 660D). A saturated calomel electrode (SCE)
and a platinum wire were used as reference electrode and counter electrode,
respectively. In all measurements, the SCE electrode was calibrated with respect to
the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE) reference scale by the following equation,
ERHE = ESCE + 0.242 + 0.0591×PH. The PH value of N2-saturated and CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution is about 8 and 7 respectively. The current density reported in this work was normalized to the geometric surface area.
2.5 CO2 reduction and products analysis
Bulk electrochemical reduction of CO2 was performed in a 50 ml
two-compartment gastight H-type cell separated by a cation exchange membrane

(Nafion 117). Each compartment contained 25 ml 0.1 M KHCO3 electrolyte, and the volume of the headspace is approximately 25 ml. The as-synthesized Cu2Cd/Cd/Cu electrode was used as working electrode and immersed into electrolyte with 1 cm2
exposed area. The electrochemical behavior of Cu2Cd/Cd/Cu electrode was evaluated by linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) with the scan rate of 20 mV s-1 in 0.1 M KHCO3 solution saturated with either N2 or CO2. CO2 was continuously purged at a rate of 20 ml min-1 for 30 minutes before each experiment, to attain saturation of the electrolyte. Then the flow rate was decreased to 5 ml min-1, during which electrochemical
reduction was conducted. The reduction potential of CO2 ranged from -1.45 V to -1.85 V (vs. SCE) to find the optimal potential for the CO2RR, and the potential was fixed at -1.65 V because the faradaic efficiency of CO was maximized in the experiment.
The gas products generated by the electrochemical reduction of CO2 were analyzed by using a gas chromatograph (GC, Hengxin GC-2020) equipped with a packed
MolSieve 5A column and a packed 2KAT-plot Al2O3 column. Nitrogen was used as the carrier gas. A flame ionization detector (FID) with methanizer was used to
quantify CO, CH4, C2H4, C2H6 and C2H2, and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) was used to quantify H2. Liquid products formed during the electrolysis were analyzed off line using NMR-400M (Switzerland Bruker Corporation).

As reported [32, 46], neither individual Cu nor Cd can perform the CO2RR with high CO faradaic efficiency. Therefore, the cause for good performance of the bimetallic
catalyst could be correlated with the engagement of Cu and Cd, which forms abundant
boundaries, and thus offers numerous active sites for the CO2RR. Therefore, the Cd/Cu catalyst could efficiently convert CO2 into CO like Cu-In and Cu-Zn bimetallic catalyst. Furthermore, when compared with the Cd/Cu catalyst, the Cu2Cd/Cd/Cu has higher faradaic efficiency for CO (Fig. 6b and 6c). The improvement of the CO
faradaic efficiency may be attributed to the formation of Cu2Cd alloy which enhances the binding energy between the catalyst and *COOH.[39, 47] Therefore, the
Cu2Cd/Cd/Cu electrocatalyst exhibits good performance toward the CO2RR.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text:
In summary, we validate that the prepared Cu-Cd catalyst shows high
electrocatalytic activity and selectivity for the CO2RR. In 0.1 M KHCO3 solution, the Cu2Cd/Cd/Cu catalyst exhibits high selective conversion to CO with a faradaic efficiency of 84% at -1.0 V (vs. RHE). Such a good performance could be related to
the boundaries between Cu and Cd that could provide sufficient active sites for the
CO2RR and the formation of Cu2Cd alloy that could enhance the binding energy between the catalyst and *COOH. The Cu2Cd/Cd/Cu catalyst can be used to replace the common precious metal catalysts (such as Au and Pd) for the electrochemical
reduction of CO2 to CO. The concept of alloy engineering for bimetallic catalysts could be further extended to develop new materials with the desired control on
